intro: In the first movement of Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in B♭ minor, Op. 23, the piano opens as accompanist, playing huge chords beneath the strings’ D♭-major melody. That famous tune appears only in the introduction, and the rest of the movement is built from other melodies.

sections.label: Intro · Horns, piano chords, strings in D♭
sections.mNote: Horns open; the strings play the theme in D♭ major.

sections.label: A · Piano’s Ukrainian theme, B♭ minor
sections.mNote: The Allegro begins with a short theme in B♭ minor.

sections.label: B · Second group, piano and woodwind
sections.mNote: Wind phrases and a broad string melody in the second group

sections.label: Dev · Themes for piano and orchestra
sections.mNote: Earlier themes pass through new keys; the piano plays octaves.

sections.label: A′ · Allegro con spirito theme returns
sections.mNote: A shortened return leads back to the contrasting themes.

sections.label: Cadenza · Piano alone
sections.mNote: The piano plays earlier melodies in the cadenza.

sections.label: Link · Orchestra in B♭ major
sections.mNote: The broad second-group melody returns in B♭ major.

sections.label: Coda · Piano and orchestra, B♭ major
sections.mNote: Themes from the Allegro return in the B♭-major ending.

cues.title: Opening theme, strings and piano
cues.text: The horns play the opening. The strings then take the D♭-major melody while the piano plays large chords beneath it, so the soloist enters as an accompanist.
cues.evidence: Tonic Chord’s score analysis identifies the horn opening, the string theme in bars 7–16 and the piano’s chordal accompaniment. https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Anatoly Tchaikovsky, 1874
cues.text: In a letter of 21 November/3 December 1874, Tchaikovsky told his brother Anatoly that he was immersed in a piano concerto. He wrote that he had to “compel piano passages to come into my head”.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Anatoly Tchaikovsky, letter 372, 21 November/3 December 1874. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Allegro con spirito, first theme
cues.text: The Allegro con spirito begins in B♭ minor with a short Ukrainian tune in clipped phrases, replacing the long string melody of the introduction. The piano and orchestra exchange the tune in quick alternation.
cues.evidence: Allegro theme and its Ukrainian source: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1. Exposition and piano–orchestra exchanges: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Nadezhda von Meck, 1879
cues.text: The Allegro’s tune came from a blind street singer whom Tchaikovsky heard in Ukraine. In a letter to Nadezhda von Meck in May 1879, he recalled the singer’s accompanying instrument and said he had used part of the melody in this concerto.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky to Nadezhda von Meck, letter 1174, 6/18–13/25 May 1879, quoted under Related Works. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Three versions of the concerto
cues.text: The concerto exists in three versions: Tchaikovsky’s original of 1875, a revised score printed in 1879 and a third edition of 1889. The 1889 text is the one usually played today.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research, Piano Concerto No. 1 (Composition: first, second and third versions; Jurgenson’s ‘3me édition revue et corrigée’ of 1889). The recording’s performing edition is unspecified. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Play-through for Rubinstein, 1875
cues.text: On 5 January 1875 Tchaikovsky played the concerto to Nikolay Rubinstein and Nikolay Hubert. Rubinstein condemned it and asked for changes, which Tchaikovsky refused to make. Hans von Bülow later took the new work to Boston.
cues.evidence: The private play-through is recounted in Tchaikovsky’s letter 736 to Nadezhda von Meck, 2–3 February 1878. Date, participants and Boston première: https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1.

cues.title: Development section
cues.text: The development takes the earlier themes through new keys. Piano octaves cut across the orchestra, and short fragments of the first subject break into the more lyrical phrases. The melody of the introduction does not return in this section.
cues.evidence: First-movement development, octave writing and thematic plan: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky); https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Hans von Bülow, 1875
cues.text: The autograph score was first dedicated to Sergey Taneyev. His name was struck out and Hans von Bülow’s written in its place. In June 1875 Bülow thanked Tchaikovsky for the dedication and wrote of the concerto’s “such unsurpassed originality, such nobility, such strength”.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research, Piano Concerto No. 1 (Dedication; Composition, first version): the autograph dedication, and Bülow’s letter of 1/13 June 1875 in the site’s translation. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Recapitulation of the first subject
cues.text: The Allegro’s first tune returns in shortened form. Tchaikovsky then brings back the wind melody and rebuilds the earlier climax, this time towards B♭ major.
cues.evidence: The shortened first-subject return and B♭-major recapitulation climax are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Boston, 1875
cues.text: Bülow gave the première on 25 October 1875 at the Music Hall in Boston, with Benjamin Johnson Lang conducting. The audience received it enthusiastically, and he played it again five days later. Within weeks it had been heard in New York, Saint Petersburg and Moscow.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research, Piano Concerto No. 1 (Performances): Boston, 13/25 and 18/30 October 1875; New York, 10/22 November; Saint Petersburg, 1/13 November; Moscow, 21 November/3 December. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Cadenza
cues.text: The orchestra stops for the long cadenza. The pianist brings earlier melodies into the solo writing and later recalls the wind theme quietly in B♭ minor.
cues.evidence: First-movement cadenza and its quiet B♭-minor recollection of the second-subject theme: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nikolay Rubinstein’s performances, 1878
cues.text: Nikolay Rubinstein, who had sharply criticised the concerto in January 1875, played it in Moscow on 22 March 1878 and again in Paris that September, at the Trocadéro. In 1880 Tchaikovsky dedicated his Second Piano Concerto to him for his “magnificent” playing of the First.
cues.evidence: Tchaikovsky Research, Piano Concerto No. 1 (Performances; Dedication): Rubinstein in Moscow, 10/22 March 1878, and at the Trocadéro, 28 August/9 September 1878; the 1880 dedication of the Second Concerto. https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Piano_Concerto_No._1

cues.title: Return of the second-group melody
cues.text: After the cadenza the orchestra returns with the broad melody from the second group, now in B♭ major.
cues.evidence: Closing section after the cadenza: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky); Tonic Chord identifies the B♭-major return at bar 642, https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda in B♭ major
cues.text: Piano and orchestra take up themes from the Allegro in a short, vigorous coda. The movement ends in B♭ major with a plagal cadence, the chord of E♭ major moving to B♭.
cues.evidence: First-movement coda and concluding plagal cadence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From D♭ major to B♭ minor
transitions.from: Intro · Horns, piano chords, strings in D♭
transitions.to: A · Piano’s Ukrainian theme, B♭ minor
transitions.how: The D♭-major introduction grows quieter, and the Allegro con spirito begins in B♭ minor. After the strings’ broad tune, the piano takes up a short Ukrainian melody in clipped phrases and quick exchanges.
transitions.evidence: Introduction and exposition described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky). Ukrainian source documented at https://en.tchaikovsky-research.net/index.php?title=Piano_Concerto_No._1.

transitions.title: Woodwind phrases open the second group
transitions.from: A · Piano’s Ukrainian theme, B♭ minor
transitions.to: B · Second group, piano and woodwind
transitions.how: The second group alternates a woodwind theme with a smoother string melody in A♭ major. When the wind tune returns, piano arpeggios accompany it and carry its shorter phrases into a larger orchestral build.
transitions.evidence: First-movement second-subject group, A♭-major string melody and piano arpeggios: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Closing theme opens the development
transitions.from: B · Second group, piano and woodwind
transitions.to: Dev · Themes for piano and orchestra
transitions.how: The exposition closes in A♭ major. In the development its lyrical closing theme becomes a rising sequence, interrupted by fragments of the first subject. Piano octaves alternate with orchestral replies, and the themes move away from their earlier keys.

transitions.title: The Allegro’s first theme returns, shortened
transitions.from: Dev · Themes for piano and orchestra
transitions.to: A′ · Allegro con spirito theme returns
transitions.how: Winds and strings bring back the Allegro’s first theme. Tchaikovsky shortened its return and gave the piano octave writing on the way to the second group. The later orchestral climax turns towards B♭ major.
transitions.evidence: Recapitulation scoring and octave transformation: https://tonic-chord.com/tchaikovsky-piano-concerto-no-1-analysis/. B♭-major climax: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Deceptive cadence into the solo cadenza
transitions.from: A′ · Allegro con spirito theme returns
transitions.how: A deceptive cadence cuts off the B♭-major climax and turns away from the expected home chord. The orchestra stops, and the pianist plays the long cadenza alone. Later, fragments of the wind theme return quietly in B♭ minor.

transitions.title: B♭ major orchestral re-entry after cadenza
transitions.how: The orchestra enters after the cadenza with the broad second-group melody in B♭ major. Sustained orchestral notes rejoin the piano, and the returning tune begins the approach to the coda.
transitions.evidence: Orchestral re-entry with the second group’s lyrical theme: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

transitions.title: Coda and close in B♭ major
transitions.to: Coda · Piano and orchestra, B♭ major
transitions.how: Piano and orchestra gather speed and force on the Allegro’s first and second themes. The short coda ends in B♭ major on a plagal cadence, with E♭ major resolving to B♭.
transitions.evidence: The coda’s themes, B♭-major close and plagal cadence are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._1_(Tchaikovsky).

composer.epithet: Composer who could write a brilliant ballroom scene and, within it, a single unguarded melody showing that someone present was unhappy.
facts: School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck: an allowance, 1877–90, and a friendship conducted by letter
Three ballets; Eugene Onegin, The Queen of Spades and other operas
composer.background:
At Kamenka on 6 July 1878, Tchaikovsky was explaining to Nadezhda von Meck how he composed. Ideas came to him in the middle of conversations, and he kept them in his head until he could sketch them on the first sheet of paper to hand. He held that waiting for the right mood was no way to work. “Inspiration is a guest who does not like to visit the idle,” he told her. He then stopped for dinner. At two o’clock he resumed, and went on to sketching, orchestration, fair copies and how far a symphony must keep to its traditional form.

He was born in Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. He grew deeply attached to his French governess, Fanny Dürbach, and began piano lessons at the end of 1845. The profession chosen for him was the law. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg. Four years later his mother died of cholera. He graduated in 1859 and took a post at the Ministry of Justice, while giving more and more of his time to opera and concerts.
